title: How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market: Now Revised & Updated for the 21st Century
author: Nicolas Darvas, with commentary by Steve Burns
summary:
This updated edition pairs Nicolas Darvas's original 1960 memoir-meets-trading-manual with new "Insights by Steve Burns" commentary chapters inserted after each of Darvas's original chapters, aiming to test whether a trading system developed by a professional ballroom dancer with no financial training, using paper tape and international cables in the 1950s, still holds up in modern markets shaped by algorithmic trading, instant information, and vastly different market structure. The original narrative remains the spine of the book: Darvas recounts how a single stock payment for a dance performance ($3,000 worth of shares that unexpectedly returned $8,000) pulled him into the market with no prior knowledge, and how he spent the following years teaching himself to trade while touring internationally as a professional dancer, with no office, no financial background, and often no more information than a hotel room newspaper and telegraphed stock quotes.

The book's narrative arc follows Darvas's own trial-and-error evolution as a trader across four distinct phases, which structure the book's original chapters: first as a naive "gambler" trading on tips and rumors with no system at all and losing money; then as a "fundamentalist" trying to pick stocks based on company fundamentals and industry reports, with limited success; then as a "technician" after he begins tracking price and volume behavior directly rather than company fundamentals, leading to his development of what became known as the Box Theory; and finally as a "techno-fundamentalist," combining technical price-action signals with a baseline fundamental screen (strong recent and projected earnings) as a final filter before trading.

The heart of Darvas's system, the Box Theory, treats a stock's price action as moving within a series of defined price "boxes" — ranges the stock trades within before either breaking out to a new, higher box (a buy signal) or falling back through the bottom of its current box (a sell signal, triggering an automatic stop-loss). Darvas combined this box-based entry and exit discipline with strict risk management via automatic stop-loss orders (essential given that he was often traveling and unable to watch the market in real time), a focus on stocks making new highs on strong volume rather than "cheap" or beaten-down stocks, and a disciplined refusal to average down into losing positions.

Steve Burns's added commentary chapters work through each of Darvas's original chapters, translating Darvas's mid-20th-century tools (paper ticker tape, telegraphed cables, print newspaper quotes) into their modern equivalents (real-time charting software, stock screeners, online brokerages), while arguing that the underlying principles — trading with the trend, cutting losses quickly and automatically, letting winners run, requiring both technical strength and fundamental quality before entering a position — remain sound regardless of the specific tools available. The book closes, as the original did, with Darvas's account of surviving two major personal financial crises during his trading career (steep losing streaks that tested and ultimately reinforced his stop-loss discipline) before crossing the two-million-dollar mark, along with the original's appendix covering his Time magazine interview.

sections.title: Canadian Period / Chapter 1 (The Gambler)
sections.summary:
This opening chapter, following the book's original chronological structure, introduces Darvas as a complete novice: a professional ballroom dancer with no financial background who receives stock as payment for a performance and, after an unexpected windfall, decides to try his hand at trading with essentially no system at all. It opens by establishing his total lack of preparation — no training, no strategy, trading largely on tips and rumors from acquaintances.

The chapter's substance follows his early, largely unsuccessful trading during this period, driven by speculation and hearsay rather than any disciplined method, establishing the losses and confusion that motivate his search for a better approach in the chapters that follow.

The chapter closes with Darvas recognizing that trading on tips and rumor is not a viable long-term strategy, setting up his shift toward researching company fundamentals in the following chapter.
keyLessons: Trading based on tips, rumors, or secondhand information without a system reliably produces losses, even for an otherwise intelligent and motivated person.
Early trading losses, if honestly examined rather than repeated, can become the motivation for developing real discipline.
Darvas's total lack of financial background is presented as evidence that a workable system, not insider expertise, is what actually separates successful from unsuccessful trading.

sections.title: Entering Wall Street / My First Crisis (The Fundamentalist)
sections.summary:
This section covers Darvas's shift toward fundamental analysis — attempting to select stocks based on company financials, earnings, and industry reports — and the financial crisis this approach eventually produces. It opens with Darvas's belief that rigorous research into company fundamentals would succeed where tip-based speculation had failed.

The chapter's substance follows his deepening study of financial reports and industry analysis, and his growing frustration as this approach, while more rigorous than his earlier gambling, still failed to reliably predict which stocks would actually perform well in the market, since strong fundamentals did not always translate into strong, timely price movement.

The chapter closes with what Darvas calls his first major crisis — a serious financial setback that forces him to question whether fundamental analysis alone, disconnected from actual price behavior, is sufficient for trading decisions, setting up his shift toward technical analysis in the following chapters.
keyLessons: Strong company fundamentals do not reliably predict short-to-medium-term stock price movement, a key insight motivating Darvas's later shift to technical analysis.
Rigorous research alone, without attention to actual market price behavior, was insufficient for Darvas's trading success.
A serious financial setback ("first crisis") functioned as the forcing event that pushed Darvas to fundamentally rethink his approach.

sections.title: Developing the Box Theory / Cables Round the World (The Technician)
sections.summary:
This section covers the development of Darvas's signature Box Theory, the technical framework at the core of his trading system. It opens with Darvas's shift in attention from company fundamentals to the stock's own price and volume behavior, observing that stocks tend to trade within identifiable price ranges before breaking decisively higher or lower.

The chapter's substance details the mechanics of the Box Theory: a stock trading within a defined price range or "box," with a breakout above the box top serving as a buy signal and a break below the box bottom serving as an automatic sell/stop-loss signal, and describes the logistical challenge of trading this system while touring internationally as a dancer, relying on cabled updates and delayed information rather than continuous market access.

The chapter closes by establishing the Box Theory as Darvas's central working method going forward, setting up the following chapter's account of combining this technical framework with a fundamental screen.
keyLessons: Stock prices tend to move within identifiable trading ranges ("boxes") before breaking decisively in one direction.
A breakout above a defined price range functioned as Darvas's buy signal; a breakdown below it functioned as an automatic stop-loss/sell signal.
Darvas developed and traded this system despite limited, delayed access to market information, relying on strict, predefined rules rather than continuous market-watching.

sections.title: During the Baby-Bear Market / The Theory Starts to Work (The Techno-Fundamentalist)
sections.summary:
This section covers Darvas's synthesis of technical and fundamental analysis into a combined system, and the period in which this combined approach begins to produce consistent results, including through a difficult ("baby-bear") market period. It opens with Darvas layering a fundamental screen — strong recent and projected company earnings — on top of his existing Box Theory technical signals, rather than relying on price action alone.

The chapter's substance describes how this combined "techno-fundamentalist" approach — requiring both a fundamentally strong company and a confirmed technical breakout before entering a position — began producing more consistent results than either approach alone had, including some success trading through a genuinely difficult market environment.

The chapter closes with the combined system beginning to demonstrably work, setting up the following chapters' account of Darvas's first major financial milestones as the system scales.
keyLessons: Combining fundamental quality (strong earnings) with technical confirmation (a Box Theory breakout) produced more reliable results than either approach used alone.
The combined system was tested and refined, in part, during a genuinely difficult market period rather than only during favorable conditions.
Requiring both technical and fundamental confirmation before entering a position functioned as an additional filter reducing false signals.

sections.title: My First Half-Million / My Second Crisis (Testing the System at Scale)
sections.summary:
This section covers Darvas's rapid early success using his combined system, reaching his first half-million dollars, followed by a second serious financial crisis that tests his discipline under the pressure of managing significantly larger sums. It opens with an account of the combined system producing a rapid string of successful trades as Darvas's account grows substantially.

The chapter's substance then turns to a second period of serious losses, which Darvas attributes largely to lapses in his own discipline — deviating from his stop-loss rules or box-based entry criteria under the pressure and overconfidence that came with early success — rather than any fundamental flaw in the system itself.

The chapter closes with Darvas recommitting to strict adherence to his own rules after this second crisis, framing consistent discipline, more than the specific technical rules themselves, as the deciding factor in his eventual success.
keyLessons: Rapid early success can create overconfidence that leads to deviation from a proven system's rules.
Darvas attributes his second major financial crisis primarily to lapses in personal discipline rather than a flaw in the underlying system.
Recommitting to strict rule adherence, especially around stop-losses, is presented as the deciding factor separating his eventual sustained success from his earlier losses.

sections.title: Two Million Dollars / Interview with Time Magazine (Culmination and Public Attention)
sections.summary:
This closing section covers Darvas crossing the two-million-dollar mark and the resulting public attention, including the Time magazine feature that first brought his story to wide public notice and led to the writing of the original book. It opens with an account of his trading system, now consistently and disciplined applied, compounding his account past the two-million-dollar milestone within roughly eighteen months from his starting capital.

The chapter's substance includes the transcribed interview with Time magazine, in which Darvas is asked to explain his unusual path to trading success as a dancer with no financial background, providing an outside, contemporaneous perspective on his story distinct from his own first-person narrative.

The chapter, and the original book, closes with this public validation of Darvas's results and system, framing the entire preceding narrative — from naive gambler through fundamentalist, technician, and finally techno-fundamentalist — as the hard-won path to a system any disciplined reader could theoretically replicate.
keyLessons: Darvas's full journey from novice to disciplined, successful trader took years of iterative failure and system refinement, not a single insight.
Public validation (the Time magazine feature) is presented as confirming the results but not substituting for understanding the underlying discipline required.
The book closes by framing its entire narrative arc as a repeatable system rather than a story of unique personal luck.
Trading on tips or rumors without a defined system reliably produces losses, regardless of a trader's intelligence or motivation.
Strong company fundamentals alone do not reliably predict near-term stock price movement.
Stocks tend to trade within identifiable price ranges ("boxes") before breaking out in one direction, forming the basis for disciplined entry and exit rules.
Combining technical confirmation (a box breakout) with a fundamental screen (strong earnings) produces more reliable signals than either approach alone.
Strict, automatic stop-loss discipline is essential, especially for traders who cannot watch the market continuously.
Rapid early success can create overconfidence that leads to costly deviations from a proven system's rules.
Recommitting to strict rule adherence after a setback is often the deciding factor separating sustained success from repeated failure.
A trading system developed under one era's market conditions and tools can remain conceptually sound even as the specific tools available change dramatically.

quotes.text: There is no reason to sell a rising stock
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: There are no good or bad stocks, there are only rising and falling stocks.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I did not know it but I was already coming up against one of the great pitfalls of the small operator -- the almost insoluble problem of when to enter the market.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: There is no sure thing in the market -- I was bound to be wrong half of the time.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I knew that being right half of the time was not the answer to success. I began to understand how I could break even and still go broke. There was only one answer to this danger: My profits had to be bigger than my losses.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I listened eagerly to what they had to say and religiously followed their tips. Whatever I was told to buy, I bought. It took me a long time to discover that this is one method that never works.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: The truth was that as my pocket had strengthened, my head had weakened.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I started to realize that stock movements were not completely haphazard. Stocks did not fly like balloons in any direction. As if attracted by a magnet, they had a defined upward or downward trend which once established, tended to continue.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I saw reasons for this; buying tended to generate more buying and progressively higher prices. Conversely, selling at a given price soon exhausts the supply of buyers available at that price, and forces offerings at a lower price -- and this process, too, tends to be progressive.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: Within this trend stocks moved in a series of frames, or what I began to call 'boxes'.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: They would oscillate fairly consistently between a low and a high point. The area which enclosed the up-and-down movement represented the box or frame.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: The task was to define the frame exactly and be sure the stock did not move decisively below the lower edge of the box. If it did, I sold it at once, because it was not acting right.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: While it stayed within its box, I considered a reaction from 55 to 50 as quite normal. It did not mean to me that the stock was going to fall back. Just the contrary.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: It shakes out the weak and frightened stock holders who mistake this reaction for a drop, and enables the stock to advance more rapidly.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I built a fortune with serenity by avoiding premature selling yet making an exodus from most of my stocks with the use of a single tool: the trailing stop-loss.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I have discovered no loss-free Nirvana. But I have been able to limit my losses to less than 10 percent wherever possible. My stop loss method had two effects. It got me out of the wrong stock and into the right one.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I decided to give 'on stop' orders to buy at a certain figure with an automatic 'stop-loss' order on them in case the stock went down. This way, I figured, I would never sleep with a loss. If any of my stocks went below the price I thought they should, I would not own them when I went to bed that night.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I knew that many times I would be 'stopped out' for the sake of a point just to see my stock climb up immediately after. But I realized that this was not so important as stopping the big losses.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I always sold too quickly because I am a coward. I decided that since I could not train myself not to get scared every time, it was better to adopt another method. This was to hold on to a rising stock but, at the same time, keep raising my stop-loss order parallel with its rise.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: If you find your automatic stop loss selling you out of everything, and the stocks you are watching are not moving towards higher boxes, then it is a signal that the market has changed.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: Profits are a function of time, and so good reasons have to exist to keep a profitless purchase longer than three weeks.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: Like human beings, stocks behave differently. Some of them are calm, slow, conservative. Others are jumpy, nervous, tense. Some of them I found easy to predict. They were consistent in their moves, logical in their behavior. They were like dependable friends.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I would select stocks on their technical action in the market, but I would only buy them when I could give improving earning power as my fundamental reason for doing so.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: I was constantly searching for the stocks that would climb into the stratosphere because of the vision of their future.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: From then on, I made up my mind to keep watching the Dow-Jones Industrial Average, but only in order to determine whether I was in a strong or a weak market.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: Whenever I bought a stock, I wrote down my reason for doing so. I did the same when I sold it.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

quotes.text: Rothschild had an agent who, as soon as victory was certain, set off for London and informed Rothschild. Rothschild started buying every British government share he could before anyone else heard the news. When they did, of course, the shares rocketed and Rothschild sold at a huge profit.
quotes.attribution: Nicolas Darvas, How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Box Theory
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Darvas's core technical framework, treating a stock's price action as moving within a series of defined price ranges or "boxes." A breakout above the top of a stock's current box is treated as a buy signal, while a break below the bottom of the box triggers an automatic stop-loss/sell signal, giving Darvas a mechanical, rules-based method for both entries and exits.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Developing the Box Theory / Cables Round the World

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Techno-Fundamentalist Approach
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Darvas's synthesized method, combining a fundamental screen (favoring companies with strong recent and projected earnings) with technical confirmation (a Box Theory breakout) before entering a trade, on the reasoning that neither fundamentals nor technicals alone were sufficiently reliable, but the combination filtered out many false signals produced by either approach individually.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: During the Baby-Bear Market / The Theory Starts to Work

actionSteps: For one stock or asset you follow, try identifying its recent trading "box" (the price range it has stayed within recently) and note what price level would represent a genuine breakout above it.
Before your next trade, write down a specific stop-loss price in advance, and commit to honoring it automatically rather than deciding in the moment.
Screen for one potential investment using both a fundamental filter (recent earnings trend) and a technical filter (recent price strength) rather than relying on either alone.

Review your own trading or investing history for one instance where overconfidence after a win led you to deviate from your own stated rules, and write down what specifically you would do differently.
If you don't currently have a written, specific set of entry and exit rules for your own investing, draft one this week, however simple, rather than continuing to decide case-by-case.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your own financial decision-making do you currently rely on tips, hearsay, or general sentiment rather than a defined, repeatable process?
Have you ever deviated from your own financial rules after an early win, and what did that cost you?
What would it take for you to trust a mechanical stop-loss rule enough to honor it automatically, even when your gut disagrees in the moment?

points: Darvas achieved his results during a specific, favorable bull market period in the 1950s; critics have long noted that a trend-following, momentum-based system like the Box Theory performs very differently in choppy, sideways, or bear market conditions than it did in the environment Darvas traded through, a point Steve Burns's added commentary explicitly attempts to address for modern readers but which remains a fair structural critique of any single-decade track record.

The book is fundamentally a survivorship-biased success story: it recounts one trader's eventual success in vivid detail but does not, and structurally cannot, account for other traders who applied similar trend-following, momentum-based approaches without achieving comparable results.

Darvas's own account includes two significant financial crises even within his own celebrated run, which is sometimes underplayed in popular retellings of the book's "made $2 million" headline; the book itself, to its credit, does not hide these losses, but readers drawn in mainly by the title may underweight how much risk and drawdown was actually involved along the way.

The original text's specific stock examples and market references are, by the authors' own acknowledgment, from a bygone market era (companies no longer trading, a pre-digital information environment); Burns's updated commentary chapters are the book's explicit mechanism for bridging this gap, but the degree to which mid-20th-century market structure lessons transfer cleanly to today's algorithmically-influenced markets remains a reasonable point of ongoing debate among traders.
criticalTake.contextNote: The book has remained continuously in print and influential in trading and technical analysis circles for over six decades, with the Box Theory frequently cited as an early precursor to later, more formalized trend-following and momentum trading systems.

whoThisIsFor: Active or aspiring individual stock traders interested in technical analysis and trend-following, and readers interested in trading history and psychology as much as strict how-to instruction.
whenToReadThis: Useful when developing or refining a personal trading system, particularly for readers who already have some basic market experience and want to study a historically influential trend-following approach.

authorBio.name: Nicolas Darvas
authorBio.bio:
Nicolas Darvas (1920–1977) was a Hungarian-born dancer, self-taught investor, and author, trained originally as an economist at the University of Budapest before fleeing Hungary in 1943 amid the upheaval of the Second World War. He went on to become one of the highest-paid professional dancers in show business, touring internationally with his dance partner, his half-sister Julia.

Darvas became involved in the stock market almost by accident, after being paid in company shares for a dance performance, and taught himself to trade over subsequent years while continuing his international dance career, developing his Box Theory system largely through self-directed study and iterative trial and error rather than any formal financial training.

His story gained wide public attention after a 1959 feature in Time magazine, which led directly to the writing and publication of "How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market" in 1960 — a book that sold close to 200,000 copies within its first eight weeks and has remained continuously influential in technical trading circles since.
notableWorks: Wall Street: The Other Las Vegas
You Can Still Make It in the Market

sourceNotes:
Synthesis based on the verified original 10-chapter structure of Darvas's 1960 book (via Wikipedia's documented chapter list and an archived full-text scan), publisher and retailer descriptions confirming this updated edition's format of alternating original chapters with Steve Burns's added "Insights by Steve Burns" commentary chapters, and biographical detail on Darvas from Wikipedia and multiple bookseller sources. Quote verification was limited to lines confirmed via accessible front-matter and preview excerpts; the full body text of both Darvas's original chapters and Burns's added commentary was not independently re-verified line-by-line in this research pass, so the quote count is intentionally conservative rather than padded — see the flag under Highlights & Quotes.

Session 24 (quote retrofit round 3): discarded the prior on-file quote attributed to "Publisher's description" -- confirmed jacket copy, not manuscript text, the same publisher-blurb-as-quote issue flagged elsewhere. Could not re-confirm the other prior on-file quote ("How to find what stocks to buy? You could not pick them out with a pin...") this pass -- it didn't surface in either primary source checked, so it's dropped as unverified-this-pass rather than re-affirmed; it may still be genuine and could be re-added if independently verified later. Sourced 27 new quotes from Goodreads' work page (ID 174151) and two independent book-notes blogs (whatheheckaboom.wordpress.com, financetrends.blogspot.com) that quote at length with page citations; cross-source overlap where it existed gave good confidence. No contamination risk -- only one Darvas book in this library.
